_comment: How each place of the catalogue's words-11.jsonl was settled before it went in config/figures-seen/: two readers read every place against its BSB verse, one asking whether the figure is plainly there and one whether the marked words, form and tags are right; a place both passed is kept as handed over, and any place either questioned was read a third time and kept, changed or dropped. A new form stands only where a reader proposed it. Places not read are held, not listed. Stray punctuation before marked words is trimmed, and Strong's tags that light the article (G3588) or the object marker (H0853), or number eight, the search's limit, are taken off as a stretch of words.

Then kept figures of speech were read again by two readers, a third settling any difference ("words re-read" counts them: those a sample showed at risk, such as wide spans, or those found only in the Hebrew or Greek that carry no tags): each kept as it was, cut to the words that carry the figure, or dropped ("words").

An alphabet poem (acrostic) lies in the Hebrew, so each kept acrostic carries the Strong's tag of its verse's first Hebrew word, the word that begins with the verse's letter, and the display shows that word lit in the Hebrew line ("tagged"); a place whose first word's root comes again in the verse is dropped, since its tag would light more than that word.

Last, a sample of 25 kept places was read by two more readers, a third settling any split; the file goes in only when 24 or more pass, and any place that fails is dropped. "samples" lists each sample and its result.
A place whose verse already has the same form from an earlier file is left out here, since the earlier file's place stands ("same form already on this verse").
Where a sample's verdict on one place held as well for kept places it did not draw, those were dropped too ("dropped as a sample's finding").

places.why: Prose. YHWH spelled backwards by the first letters of four Hebrew words is a hidden acrostic, not an alphabet run, and the whole verse is marked.
Prose request. YHWH spelled by four first letters is a hidden acrostic. No alphabet runs through the passage.
Prose speech. YHWH read backwards from four last letters is a hidden acrostic, not plain.
Narrative prose. Four final letters spelling YHWH is a hidden acrostic, and the whole verse is marked.

In the Hebrew, both lines of this verse begin with aleph (אֶשְׂמְחָה "I will be glad", אֲזַמְּרָה "I will sing praise"). But that is just the Hebrew "I will" prefix, and nothing in this verse alone shows an alphabet poem. The alphabet appears only by reading across Psalms 9 and 10, and it is broken there: dalet is missing, and lines opening with ki (9:4 "For You have upheld", 9:12 "For the Avenger") break in. A BSB reader would not see it, and even a reader of the Hebrew would need a note to find it at 9:2. The verse is also the second half of the aleph group that begins at 9:1, and only one of its two aleph words is tagged. In doubt, so it fails.

Psalms 9 and 10 run the alphabet only across both psalms, with letters missing and lines that break in, so even a reader of the Hebrew would need a note to see it at this verse (the second sample failed Psalm 9:2 for this); every acrostic place of the two psalms is dropped

The Hebrew verse opens with 'elohai (aleph), repeating the aleph of 25:1. The beth comes only at the second word (be-kha), so the verse's own opening does not plainly follow the letter before.
The verse opens with resh (רְאֵה), but 25:17 opens with tsade, so qof is skipped. 25:19 also opens with resh (רְאֵה). The run breaks at this pair, so it is not plain which verse holds the resh place.
The verse opens with resh (רְאֵה), the same letter as 25:18. Qof is missing and resh comes twice, so this verse does not plainly take the letter after the one before.

The verse opens with vav (וְהִתְעַנַּג), which is only the conjunction "and". The acrostic in Psalm 37 runs by pairs of verses: 37:3 opens the bet pair and 37:5 opens gimel, so this verse carries no letter.
The verse opens with vav (וְהוֹצִיא), the conjunction "and". It is the second verse of the gimel pair begun in 37:5, and dalet opens 37:7, so this verse does not carry a letter of the alphabet.
The verse opens with kaf (כִּי, "for"), which is not the next letter. It is the second verse of the he pair begun by הֶרֶף in 37:8, and the vav pair begins at 37:10.

The verse opens with vav (וַעֲנָוִים, "and humble"), the conjunction. That repeats the vav of 37:10 as the second verse of that pair, and zayin opens 37:12. So the verse does not take the next letter.
The verse opens with aleph (אֲדֹנָי), which breaks the run between the zayin of 37:12 and the chet of 37:14. It is the second verse of the zayin pair and carries no letter of the acrostic.
Opens with charbam (chet). That is the second verse of the chet pair begun at 37:14 and not the next letter, so no acrostic letter falls on this verse.
Opens with ki (kaf). It is the second verse of the tet pair begun at 37:16 and does not carry the next letter.
Opens with lo (lamed). That is out of order between yod at 37:18 and kaf at 37:20, and the verse is the second of the yod pair.
Opens with ki (kaf). It is the second verse of the lamed pair begun at 37:21, so the run of letters does not fall here.
Opens with ki (kaf), not nun. It is the second verse of the mem pair begun at 37:23.
Opens with kol (kaf), out of order. It is the second verse of the nun pair begun at 37:25, and samek begins 37:27.
Opens with ki (kaf). The ayin is at best hidden inside the verse (le'olam), not at the start of a line, so it is not plain.
Opens with tsaddiqim (tsade). That comes before pe at 37:30 and is out of order, so the verse does not show the run of letters.
Opens with torat (tav), out of order. It is the second verse of the pe pair begun at 37:30.
Opens with YHWH (yod), out of order. It finishes the tsade pair begun at 37:32, and qof begins 37:34.
Opens with vaya'avor (vav), out of order. It is the second verse of the resh pair begun at 37:35.
Opens with ufosh'im (vav). It is the second verse of the shin pair begun at 37:37 and carries no next letter.

Opens with ut'shu'at, whose first letter is the conjunction vav; the tav comes only after it. The verse does not plainly begin with the letter, so when in doubt it stays out. The whole verse is also marked rather than the opening word.
Opens with vaya'zrem (vav). It is the second verse of the closing pair and begins no letter of the run.

I checked the first Hebrew word of every verse in Lamentations 2. All 22 verses begin with the alphabet's letters in turn, from aleph (2:1 eikhah) to tav (2:22 tiqra), each letter once. The only change is that pe (2:16 patsu) comes before ayin (2:17 asah). The book shows that order itself: Lamentations 3 (pe at 3:46-48, ayin at 3:49-51) and Lamentations 4 (4:16 pe, 4:17 ayin) put the two letters the same way. So a reader of the Hebrew sees the alphabet poem plainly, and this verse holds its letter's place in it. Marking the whole verse follows the convention for acrostic places. There are no Strong's tags to remove.

"Remember me favorably, O my God" is Nehemiah praying to God, who hears him. The address does change from the reader to God, but God is not someone absent, and an earlier ruling held that a prayer to God present is not plainly apostrophe. The mark also takes in the request, not only the address.

"O my God, remember Tobiah and Sanballat" is a plain prayer to the God who hears. It is not speech to someone absent, so the label would mislead a reader, and the figure is not plain. The marked words also stop at a dangling verb.
"Remember me for this, O my God" is Nehemiah's ordinary prayer inside his memoir, spoken to the God who hears. A turn to God present is not plainly a turn to someone absent, so it does not go live.
"Remember me for this as well, O my God, and show me mercy" is a real request to God in mid-account. God is not absent, so "turning to speak to someone absent" is not plainly shown.
"Remember them, O my God" is Nehemiah praying to God about the priests who defiled the priesthood. It is a prayer to the God who hears, not plainly speech to someone absent.
"Remember me, O my God, with favor" is the book's closing prayer to God. It is not speech to someone absent or imaginary, so the figure is not plain.

David speaks to God in 4:1 ("Answer me when I call, O God"), then turns to the men who malign him and are not there: "How long, O men, will my honor be maligned?" The turn is plain. The vocative "O men" carries the address, while "How long" belongs to the question, so the mark is "O men".

"Sing to the LORD, O you His saints" calls the worshippers, who are most likely the very people singing the psalm. Nothing shows them absent. It is a call to worship, not plainly an apostrophe, and the mark takes in the command as well.
"Love the LORD, all His saints" is the psalm's plain call to the faithful who hear it. Nothing in the verse shows them absent, so the figure is not plain.
"Be strong and courageous, all you who hope in the LORD" goes on with the call to the faithful begun in 31:23. This verse has no turn and no one absent, and the mark is the whole verse.
same form already on this verse (psalm-34-12-question-seen)

The verse carries on the address to the mighty man begun in 52:1 and does not turn from any hearer. That the man is absent is not plain from the words, and "tongue" put for the man is a second figure, so speaking to the absent is not plain here.

"Do you indeed speak justly, O rulers?" opens the psalm, so there is no turn away from other hearers. Nothing in the verse plainly shows the rulers are absent. When in doubt, the place does not go live.
"Rest in God alone, O my soul" is the psalmist speaking to himself. His soul is not someone absent, so the label does not fit.
"O you who love the LORD" calls on the worshippers, who are the psalm's own hearers and not someone absent. The marked words also take in the command "Hate evil".
"Bless the LORD, O my soul" is the psalmist speaking to himself, carried on from 103:1. His soul is not absent.
"Bless the LORD, O my soul" is the psalmist speaking to himself, not turning to someone or something absent.

Between speaking to God in 108:1 and 108:3, the psalmist turns to call on instruments that cannot hear: "Awake, O harp and lyre!" The call is to both, so the marked words should be "O harp and lyre", not "O harp" alone.

The psalmist speaks to God in 119:114 and 119:116, and in between he turns to absent evildoers: "Depart from me, you evildoers". The words "that I may" belong to the next line and carry nothing of the figure.
places.words_why: Psalm 119 speaks to God ("You are my hiding place", "Sustain me as You promised"), and here it turns to absent men: "Depart from me, you evildoers", with God in the third person ("my God"). Only the address should be lit, not the verb.

places.why: "Remember, O LORD" is a prayer to God, the psalm's real hearer, not speech to someone absent. The marked words also run on into the object "the sons of Edom".

In the middle of a prayer to God ("O God, that You would slay the wicked", then 139:20 "who speak of You"), the psalmist turns to the absent men: "away from me, you bloodthirsty men". The marked words stopped before "men".
places.words_why: In the middle of a prayer ("O God, that You would slay the wicked"), David turns to absent men: "away from me, you bloodthirsty men." Only the address should be lit.

places.why: After calling on the heavens in 148:1-6, the psalm turns to call on things of the earth that cannot hear: "all great sea creatures and ocean depths". The marked words should be that call alone, not the whole verse with its trailing comma.

"Go up, O Elam! Lay siege, O Media!" is said inside the vision that is declared to the prophet. It is a summons within the vision, not the speaker turning from his hearers to someone absent, so the figure is not plain.
Isaiah is sent to say this to Shebna in person (22:15 "Go, say to Shebna"; 22:16 "What are you doing here"), so "O mighty man" speaks to someone who is there.

"He said, 'You shall rejoice no more, O oppressed Virgin Daughter of Sidon'" reports a decree spoken to Sidon. It is reported speech, not the speaker turning from his hearers, so speaking to the absent is not plain at these words.
"Woe to you, O Ariel" speaks to Jerusalem under another name, the city of Isaiah's own hearers. The one spoken to is not plainly absent.

Jerusalem is Zion, the people these chapters are spoken to (51:16 'to say to Zion, You are My people'). The verse does not plainly turn from the hearers to someone absent, and the mark also takes in the doubled 'Awake, awake!', which is a different figure.

The call to Zion goes on with the same address to the people being comforted. The verse does not plainly show a turn to an absent hearer, and the mark takes in the command and the doubling rather than the address.
This goes on with the address to Zion from 52:1. There is no plain turn to someone absent, and the mark takes in the whole command.

After speaking of Zion's watchmen (52:8), the verse calls on ruins to sing, which cannot hear: 'sing together, O ruins of Jerusalem'. The mark 'O ruins of' breaks off before 'Jerusalem', so the whole address is given.

'O barren woman' is Zion under the picture of a childless wife, and Zion is the one comforted in these chapters. The figure in the words is the picture, not a plain turn from the hearers to someone absent. When in doubt it does not go live.
The prophet turns from 'I will wail for Moab' (48:31) to speak to a vine, which cannot hear: 'I will weep for you, O vine of Sibmah'. The mark 'O vine of' breaks off before 'Sibmah'.

The oracle concerning Edom already speaks to Edom as 'you' in 49:15, so this verse has no turn. 'O dwellers in the clefts of the rocks' names the oracle's own addressee, which is how the oracles against the nations speak, the same as Ezekiel's 'O Mount Seir'. It is not plainly a figure.
Zion calls to passers-by who are onlookers in the scene she pictures, so it is not plainly speech to someone absent. The marked words are also the question 'Is this nothing to you', not the address.

After 'The hearts of the people cry out to the Lord', the poet turns to speak to a wall, which cannot hear: 'O wall of the Daughter of Zion, let your tears run down like a river'. 'O wall' cuts the address short, so the whole address is given.
'Behold, O Tyre, I am against you' is the word the Lord GOD gives for Tyre, so Tyre is the stated addressee of the oracle. That is how the oracle speaks. It is not a plain turn to an imagined hearer.
The verse opens 'Tell Tyre ... that this is what the Lord GOD says', so Tyre is the named hearer of the message the prophet must give. The address is not to someone imagined.
'Your men of skill, O Tyre' goes on with the lament the prophet is told to give to Tyre (27:3 'Tell Tyre'). It is the same message to the same addressee, not a turn.

'You are to declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I am against you, O Sidon' is a message the prophet is told to speak to Sidon. Sidon is its stated hearer, so this is the oracle's form, not a plain figure.
'Speak to him and tell him ... Behold, I am against you, O Pharaoh' names the stated recipient of the message. It is not a turn from the hearers to an imagined one.

'Declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I am against you, O Mount Seir' is the message the prophet is sent to give against Seir (35:2). Mount Seir stands for Edom's people here (35:5), so this is how the oracle speaks, not a plain figure.
This goes on with the same message to Edom that began in 35:3, and 35:14 already speaks to it as 'you'. There is no turn away from the hearers.

The prophet is told to speak to mountains as though they could listen: 'O mountains of Israel, hear the word of the LORD.' Here the land itself is meant (36:8-9: it will bear fruit for My people and be tilled), and land cannot hear. The whole address 'O mountains of Israel' is given in place of 'O mountains'.

The land is again told to hear: 'O mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD ... to the mountains and hills, to the ravines and valleys'. Mountains cannot hear. The whole address 'O mountains of Israel' is given.
In the vision the prophet really commands the breath, and it obeys: 'the breath entered them' (37:10). It is a command that is answered in the vision, not a speaker turning aside to an absent hearer.

'Declare that this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I am against you, O Gog' is the message the prophet is told to give against Gog (38:2). Gog is its stated hearer, so this is how the oracle speaks.
'It will happen in the latter days, O Gog' goes on with the message to Gog that began in 38:3, which has spoken to him as 'you' throughout. There is no turn from the hearers.

Gog is the named addressee of the whole oracle Ezekiel is told to speak. 38:2-3 already says "Prophesy against him and declare ... I am against you, O Gog", and 39:1 repeats that commission. The speaker does not turn away from his hearers at this verse, so the figure is not plain here.

3:2-3 speak of the nations as "them" ("I will enter into judgment against them", "They cast lots for My people"). 3:4 turns to speak to the absent peoples themselves: "what do you have against Me, O Tyre, Sidon, and all the regions of Philistia?" The address is the whole vocative, not "O Tyre" alone.

The oracle turns to speak to Edom at 1:2 ("I will make you small among the nations"). In 1:3, "O dwellers in the clefts of the rocks" only goes on with that address. There is no turn at this verse, and the marked words also stop mid-line.

"Your mighty men, O Teman" goes on with the address to Edom that runs through the book from 1:2. The brief third-person question in 1:8 does not make 1:9 a plain turn to a new, absent hearer. When in doubt, the place does not go live.

"And you, O watchtower of the flock, O stronghold of the Daughter of Zion" speaks to Zion and Jerusalem, the very people Micah preaches to, and 4:9 goes on speaking to them. The verse does not plainly show that the one addressed is absent.

places.words_why: After addressing the "daughter of troops" (5:1), the prophet turns to speak to a town: "But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah." The address is carried by "you, Bethlehem Ephrathah"; the joining word "But" is not part of it.

places.why: "Sing for joy, O Daughter of Zion; shout aloud, O Israel!" calls on the prophet's own people, who are already addressed as "you" in 3:11-12. They are not absent, and the marked words also take in the verb.

The call to the exiles begins at 2:6 ("Get up! Get up! Flee from the land of the north"), and 2:7 goes on with it to the same people. Nothing turns at this verse, and the verse alone does not plainly set the hearers apart from the exiles being called. When in doubt, the place does not go live.

"Shout for joy and be glad, O Daughter of Zion, for I am coming to dwell among you" is God speaking to His own people under their usual name, not a turn to someone absent. The marked words also run into the commands.
"Rejoice greatly, O Daughter of Zion! Shout in triumph, O Daughter of Jerusalem!" calls on the prophet's own people in Jerusalem, not someone absent. The marked words also take in "Rejoice greatly".

places.words_why: Jesus is speaking to the crowds (11:7, 11:20 "began to denounce the cities") and turns to speak to towns that are not there: "Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!" The address carries the figure, not the cry "Woe to", matching "you, Capernaum" in 11:23, and both towns are addressed.

places.why: "In them the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled: 'You will be ever hearing...'" quotes a prophecy about the people. Nobody absent is spoken to, and the marked words are the whole verse. The hearing and seeing lines belong under a different form, and that would be a new place, not this one.

places.words_why: Speaking to the seventy-two, Jesus turns to absent towns: "Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!" The address carries the figure, not "Woe to", matching "you, Capernaum" in 10:15, and both towns are addressed.

places.why: "Go to this people and say, 'You will be ever hearing...'" is Paul quoting the message God gave Isaiah to speak to the people. It is not a turn to someone absent, and the marked words are the whole verse.

"So when you, O man, pass judgment on others" goes on with the address that began in 2:1, and that person may well be a reader of the letter. The verse does not plainly show someone absent. Its question already has its own place (romans-2-3-question-seen), so this one is not moved to that form.

"Now you, if you call yourself a Jew" speaks to a kind of reader who may be among the letter's readers. Nothing shows that person is absent, and the marked words are the whole verse rather than words that carry a figure.

The one spoken to is "One of you" who objects (9:19), a reader of the letter, not someone absent. The marked words "are you, O man" also cut the question in two. That question already has its own place (romans-9-20-question-seen), so this one is not moved to that form.
"So you are no longer a slave, but a son" is Paul speaking straight to the Galatians he writes to. Nobody absent is turned to, and the marked words are the whole verse.

"For it is written: 'Rejoice, O barren woman'" is Paul quoting Isaiah's call to Zion, which 4:26 calls "our mother". The barren woman stands for a people being spoken to. The verse does not plainly show the speaker turning from his hearers to someone absent.

"O foolish man" goes on with the reply to the objector of 2:18 ("someone will say"), who has been spoken to since 2:18. There is no turn at this verse, and the reader cannot plainly tell this man is absent rather than one of the readers.

"Come now, you who say, 'Today or tomorrow we will go...'" speaks to traders who may be among the readers, and nothing shows they are absent. The marked words "Come now, you who" also break off mid-phrase.

"Come now, you who are rich, weep and wail" does not show in the verse itself that the rich are absent from the readers. Only commentary could show it. The marked words "Come now, you who" also stop before "are rich".

The verse tells how the man was formed and became a living being. Nothing in its words points ahead. The foreshadowing is known only from Romans 5:14 and 1 Corinthians 15:45, so a reader of this verse alone would not see it.
A plain statement about marriage. The link to Christ and the church comes from Ephesians 5:32, not from these words, so the verse itself shows no foreshadowing.
A birth and naming record. Only Galatians 4:24 reads Hagar and her son as a figure; this verse in its own words shows none.
"at the very time God had promised" tells of a promise kept, not of something to come. The figure of the children of promise is drawn in Galatians 4, not seen here.
Plain narrative of Ishmael mocking Isaac. The figure is drawn only in Galatians 4:29; the verse's words point to nothing later.
Sarah's demand in the story. Galatians 4:30 quotes it within Paul's figure, but the Genesis verse in its own words shows no foreshadowing.
God's command in the test. The echoes of an only son offered are not stated in the verse, and Hebrews 11:19 speaks of Isaac being received back, which is not this verse. Not plain here.
A description of Jacob's dream. John 1:51 echoes it, but nothing in this verse points ahead, and Scripture does not call the ladder a figure in so many words.
"the Passover lamb" is named in its ordinary sense, as the instruction for the feast. The type is known from 1 Corinthians 5:7, not from these words.
Narrative of the LORD guiding by cloud and fire. Only 1 Corinthians 10:1-2 draws on the cloud; the verse itself shows no foreshadowing.
The crossing told plainly. The link to baptism is made in 1 Corinthians 10:2, not in these words.
"the bread that the LORD has given you" names the manna in its ordinary sense. John 6 and 1 Corinthians 10:3 are needed to see it point ahead.
"This is the blood of the covenant" is said over the covenant rite in its ordinary sense. The verse points to nothing later; Hebrews 9 is needed to see a type.

"according to the pattern I show you" says the tabernacle follows a model shown to Moses. That is a copy of a model, not a foreshadowing of something to come, and the marked words name the model, not a type.
Building by the model seen on the mountain. The verse says nothing of a later thing it points to; the "copy and shadow" reading is from Hebrews 8:5, not these words.
Narrative of the golden calf feast. It is set as a warning only in 1 Corinthians 10:7; the verse itself shows no figure.
A rule for the Day of Atonement offerings. The link to Jesus suffering outside the gate is made in Hebrews 13:11-12, not in these words.
The lampstand made after the model shown to Moses. The model is what it copies, nothing in the verse points ahead, and the marked words cut off before "Moses".
A Passover rule. The unbroken bones are seen as pointing to Christ only through John 19:36; the verse in its own words does not point ahead.
God sets Moses above the prophets of 12:6. Nothing points to a later one; Hebrews 3 compares Moses with Christ, which the verse itself does not show.
The sentence passed on the grumblers. It serves as a warning only in 1 Corinthians 10 and Hebrews 3; the verse itself shows no figure.
The striking of the rock told plainly. The rock's meaning comes from 1 Corinthians 10:4, not from these words.
Narrative of a judgment. It becomes a warning only in 1 Corinthians 10:9; the verse shows no foreshadowing.
The bronze snake on the pole told plainly. The foreshadowing is named by Jesus in John 3:14, but nothing in this verse's own words points ahead, so it is not seen in the words here.
A plain count of the dead. Only 1 Corinthians 10:8 uses it as a warning; the verse shows no figure.

In its own words, "a prophet like me", the verse makes Moses the pattern of a prophet still to come. The marked span stops on a dangling "from among", so it is cut back to the words that carry the figure.
God's words "I will raise up for them a prophet like you" plainly set Moses as the pattern of the prophet to come. The span is cut back from the dangling "from among".

On its own the verse shows only a prophet's words "fulfilled". The type reading needs Hosea 11:1, where the words are about Israel, and that is not in this verse. A reader of Matthew 2:15 sees a fulfilled prophecy, not a foreshadowing, so in doubt it does not go live.
"something greater than the temple is here" argues from lesser to greater in a dispute about the Sabbath. Nothing in the verse says the temple pointed ahead to Him.
"One greater than Jonah is here" compares greatness and sets the Ninevites against this generation. The foreshadowing is the sign in 12:39-40, not these words. The span also leaves out "One".
"One greater than Solomon is here" compares greatness in wisdom. Nothing in the passage makes Solomon point ahead to a later one, and the span leaves out "One".
Here "except the sign of Jonah" stands with no likeness drawn. The verse goes straight on to "Then He left them and went away," so the foreshadowing is explained only at 12:40, not in these words.

The verse only describes life before the flood. The pattern ("As it was ... so will it be") is stated in 24:37 and 24:39. The marked words are only a time limit and do not carry the figure, and marking the whole verse would be a stretch.

"until the flood came and swept them all away. So will it be at the coming of the Son of Man" plainly makes the flood the pattern of the coming. The span cut off "all away" and is now the whole clause about the event.

Read alone, "none will be given it except the sign of Jonah" does not say what Jonah points ahead to. Only the next verse draws the likeness to the Son of Man, and that verse is marked on its own (place 101).

"as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so the Son of Man will be a sign to this generation" (after 11:29, "the sign of Jonah") plainly makes Jonah the earlier sign of the coming one. The marked "as Jonah was" stopped mid-clause, so the whole correspondence is marked.
"One greater than Solomon is here" compares greatness to condemn this generation. The verse does not say Solomon points ahead, so no foreshadowing is plain.
"One greater than Jonah is here" compares greatness. Jonah as a sign is drawn at 11:30, not by these words.

"Just as it was in the days of Noah, so also will it be in the days of the Son of Man" plainly makes Noah's days the pattern of the coming days. The mark gave only the first half, so both halves are marked.
"up to the day Noah entered the ark" only tells what happened. The link to the Son of Man is made at 17:26, not by these words.
"It was the same in the days of Lot" likens Lot's days to Noah's days. The forward link is carried at 17:30, not in this verse.
"on the day Lot left Sodom, fire and sulfur rained down" is plain narration. Nothing in the verse points ahead.
"It will be just like that on the day the Son of Man is revealed" does not name the earlier event. Lot's day is only in the verses before, so the marked words do not hold the foreshadowing.

"Look, the Lamb of God!" said as Jesus walks by calls Him a lamb. That is plainly a metaphor. The verse names no earlier lamb pointing ahead, so it is not a type. There is no other place at this verse.
"ascending and descending on the Son of Man" echoes Jacob's dream only for a reader who already knows Genesis 28. The verse names neither Jacob nor the ladder, so the figure is not plain.

"the temple of His body" calls His body a temple, which is a metaphor, not a foreshadowing. That metaphor is already a separate place (john-2-21-metaphor-seen), so recasting this one would duplicate it.
The crowd's "Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness" recalls history. Nothing in these words points the manna ahead.
"Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died" states history to set against the bread of life. It does not plainly make the manna point ahead.

"Unlike your fathers, who ate the manna and died, the one who eats this bread will live forever" plainly sets opposites together: died against live forever. That is an antithesis, not a foreshadowing. The mark took only one half, so both are marked. The existing metaphor place here covers different words.
"will raise up for you a prophet like me", which Peter applies to Jesus (3:20, 26), plainly makes Moses the pattern of the coming prophet. The mark ended on a dangling "from among".
"God will raise up for you a prophet like me" plainly makes Moses the pattern of a coming prophet. The mark ended on a dangling "from among".
"according to the pattern he had seen" uses "pattern" in its ordinary sense: the model shown to Moses. It points back to a plan, not ahead to a later thing.
The verse opens "But the gift is not like the trespass" and argues from lesser to greater, stressing unlikeness. The mark also starts mid-clause on "died by". The pattern itself is stated at 5:14.
"if, by the trespass of the one man, death reigned ... how much more" carries on the "not like" argument from lesser to greater. The mark starts on "by" and carries no foreshadowing.

"just as one trespass brought condemnation ... so also one act of righteousness brought justification" sets two acts against each other as opposites. That the first foreshadows the second is stated in 5:14, not here, so a reader would need help to see a type in this verse.

"through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous" reads as an opposite set against an opposite. It does not plainly read as an earlier thing pointing ahead to a later one. The pattern is named in 5:14, not in this verse.

The bread "leavened with malice" and "unleavened bread of sincerity" is a metaphor in the leaven picture already marked as an allegory at 5:6-8 and a metaphor at 5:7. It is not an earlier thing pointing ahead, and the mark stops before what the bread stands for.

"They were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea" uses "baptized" in a figurative way. But the words themselves do not say the crossing points ahead to anything later, so a reader would need commentary to see a type.
The marked "same spiritual drink" carries no figure. The figure in the verse, "that rock was Christ", is already a separate metaphor place (1-corinthians-10-4-metaphor-seen).
"God was not pleased with most of them" is plain narration of the judgment. The examples are named at 10:6 and 10:11, not in these words.
"Do not be idolaters, as some of them were" is a plain warning by comparison. The events are called examples only at 10:6 and 10:11, so these words show no foreshadowing.
"as some of them did" is a plain warning by comparison. Nothing in the verse's own words makes the event point ahead.
"We should not test Christ, as some of them did" is a plain warning by comparison, not a foreshadowing shown in these words.
"do not complain, as some of them did" is a plain warning by comparison. The events are named as examples in 10:11, not in these words.

"these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us" is a plain statement in which "examples" has its ordinary sense of warnings. These words are not themselves a figure that points ahead.

The verse names neither man, so a foreshadowing is not plain here. It does plainly set death against the resurrection of the dead in two matching clauses, which is antithesis. The mark takes both halves.
places.words_why: The opposites are plain in the verse: "death came through a man" is set against "the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man." The joining word "since" does not carry the figure, so it is cut.

places.why: "as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive" plainly sets dying in Adam against being made alive in Christ, as Romans 5:19 is marked. The verse does not say that Adam points ahead, so the form is antithesis and the mark takes both halves.

"of the dust of the earth" and "from heaven" plainly set the two men's origins against each other. The verse does not say that the first man points ahead, so the form is antithesis and the mark takes both halves.
"Abraham had two sons" is the history. Paul reads it as an allegory only at 4:24, which is already marked, and the span breaks off at "one by the slave".
"His son by the slave woman was born according to the flesh" still tells the history. The cut span "was born" carries no figure of its own.

"These things serve as illustrations, for the women represent two covenants" is allegory, not a foreshadowing. A cited allegory is already marked at Galatians 4:24, so a seen place here would repeat it.
"Hagar stands for Mount Sinai" carries on the allegory already marked at 4:24, not a type. The mark "Hagar stands for" also stops before what she stands for.

Nothing in the verse foreshadows anything. But "she is our mother" plainly calls the Jerusalem above our mother, a city said to be the thing it is like. The marked "the Jerusalem above is free" carries no figure.
"you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise" is a plain, literal likeness inside Paul's allegory. It does not make Isaac point ahead, and it is no figurative simile.

Paul names the story himself in 4:24 as illustrations, so the form would be allegory, not type. The marked words also stop at "persecuted" and leave out "It is the same now", which is what shows the likeness. Too unsure to put up here.
"we are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman" is the conclusion of the allegory named in 4:24. Nothing at these words points ahead to a later thing.

2:16 is a plain list of food, drink, a feast, a New Moon and a Sabbath. The figure is stated only in 2:17 ("These are a shadow of the things to come"), and "These" covers the whole list, not just the marked words.
"just as Moses was faithful" sets two men side by side as alike in faithfulness. 3:3 goes straight on to the difference. Nothing says Moses pointed ahead to Christ.
"testifying to what would be spoken later" says Moses bore witness. That is plain statement, not a person or event shown as a pattern of a later one.

"if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day" argues that Joshua's rest was not the final rest. It does not plainly present that rest as a picture of the later one.
"the same pattern of disobedience" means an example of disobedience not to copy. Nothing points ahead to a later fulfilment.

"in the order of Melchizedek" names a priestly order in its ordinary sense, as 7:11 speaks of "the order of Aaron". The verse says the explanation is still to come (5:11) and shows no foreshadowing at these words.
"inner sanctuary behind the curtain" is where hope reaches, and Hebrews treats this as the real sanctuary. The marked words name that reality, not an earlier thing that points ahead.
"in the order of Melchizedek" names the order of His priesthood in its ordinary sense. The phrase on its own does not plainly show Melchizedek as a foreshadowing.

"one in the order of Melchizedek and not in the order of Aaron" sets two priestly orders side by side by name. The same phrase used for Aaron is plainly literal, so this one shows no foreshadowing at these words.
"in the order of Melchizedek" is quoted as testimony and names the order of the priesthood. The marked line does not show the type by itself.
"priests who offer gifts according to the law" is a plain statement of fact. The figure ("a copy and shadow") is named in 8:5, and of the place where they serve.
"the first covenant had regulations for worship and also an earthly sanctuary" is a plain description. Its meaning as a figure is given later in the chapter, not in this verse.
"the cherubim of glory, overshadowing the mercy seat" describes the ark, and "overshadowing" is literal. The writer adds "we cannot discuss these things in detail now".
"the priests entered regularly into the first room" is a plain description. Only 9:8 to 9 give it a meaning, and this verse names nothing later that it points to.
"only the high priest entered the second room" is a plain description. The figure is drawn out in 9:8 to 9 and 9:11 to 12, not at these words.
"until the time of reform" puts a time limit on the regulations. It is not a person, thing or event that points ahead.
"greater and more perfect tabernacle" names the heavenly reality itself, not the earlier figure. The type is only implied by the comparison.

"He did not enter by the blood of goats and calves, but ... by His own blood" sets two means side by side and rules one out. The verse does not itself say the animal blood pointed ahead. The figure is named at 9:9 and 9:23 to 24, so this one stays down.
"he sprinkled with blood the tabernacle" is a plain account of what Moses did. The figure is drawn out in 9:23, not at these words.
"nearly everything must be purified with blood" states a rule of the law plainly. It is not a figure.

"copies of the heavenly things" states outright that earthly things copy heavenly ones that exist now. That is not an earlier thing pointing ahead to a later one, and the words are used in their plain sense.

"as the high priest enters the Most Holy Place every year" sets Christ against the high priest to show a difference ("Nor did He ... again and again"). The pattern is named in 9:24 ("a man-made copy"), not at these words. Too unsure for an unsourced type.

"the curtain of His body" plainly calls His body the curtain through which the way into the Most Holy Place (10:19) is opened. His body is said to be the thing it is like, which is a metaphor. The verse does not itself name the tabernacle curtain as an earlier thing pointing ahead, so the form is metaphor, not type.
"We have an altar" does not say what the altar is, and readers differ on that. The marked words also break off on a stray "from which".

"the bodies are burned outside the camp" describes only the sacrifice practice in this verse. The link to Jesus comes only in the next verse ("And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate"), so this verse alone does not show the type.
"let us go to Him outside the camp" is a call drawn from 13:11-12, not an earlier person or event pointing ahead. What the camp stands for is not named, so no figure is plain here.

"the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot" says outright that Christ is a lamb, so the metaphor is plain. The earlier lamb is not named in the verse, so calling it a type is less plain.

3:21 says "this water symbolizes the baptism", so the type is plain. It is carried by the eight being "saved through water". The marked "days of Noah while the ark" is only the setting, cut off mid-clause.
The shepherd picture runs plainly from "The LORD is my shepherd" through green pastures, quiet waters and "Your rod and Your staff". The title "A Psalm of David." is no part of the picture.
places.words_why: "The LORD is my shepherd" begins a picture that carries on into "green pastures" and "quiet waters" (23:2). "I shall not want" is plain speech, not part of the picture.

places.why: "Sing about a fruitful vineyard" begins a picture carried through 27:3-5 (keeper, watering, thorns and briers). 27:6 applies it to Jacob and Israel. The opening "In that day:" and the opening quotation mark are left out.
places.words_why: The vineyard picture continues with "I, the LORD, am its keeper; I water it" (27:3), and 27:6 names Jacob and Israel taking root. The picture itself is "a fruitful vineyard", not "Sing about".

places.why: Verse 1 is a question and its answer about a warrior from Edom. The winepress picture begins only in 63:2 as a likeness, and "It is I, proclaiming vindication, mighty to save" is no picture, so no picture carried through plainly starts here.

The vine-wood picture runs through 15:2-5, and 15:6 applies it ("Like the wood of the vine ... so I will give up the people of Jerusalem"). The quotation mark and the address "Son of man," are left out.
places.words_why: The vine picture runs through the chapter, and 15:6 explains it: "Like the wood of the vine among the trees of the forest ... so I will give up the people of Jerusalem." The picture's words are "the wood of the vine".

places.why: Jerusalem's birth and parents begin the picture of a foundling girl carried on through the chapter (16:4-8). The narration "and tell her that this is what the Lord GOD says to Jerusalem:" is left out.
places.words_why: Jerusalem is given parents, "Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite", and the next verse carries on the picture of her birth ("your cord was not cut"). "Your origin and your birth were in the land of the Canaanites" can be read as plain speech, so it is left out.

places.why: The lioness and her cubs begin a lament for "the princes of Israel" (19:1), carried on to the cub caged with hooks and brought "to the king of Babylon" (19:9). The narration "and say:" and the quotation mark are left out.

"the house of Israel has become dross to Me" begins the smelting picture carried on through 22:19-22 ("As silver is melted in a furnace, so you will be melted"). The quotation mark and the address "Son of man," are left out.

The two sister women are carried through Ezekiel 23, and 23:4 explains them itself: "Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem." The address "Son of man," is not part of the picture, so the words start at "there were two women".

The text calls this a parable, and 24:6 says the pot is the city ("Woe to the city of bloodshed, to the pot now rusted"). A pot that stands for the city fits "a picture carried through" better than "a story that teaches", since there is no story here, only commands about the pot. Line 1 only introduces the picture, so the words are lines 2 and 3.
The shepherds and the flock run through Ezekiel 34, and 34:31 explains the flock: "You are My flock, the sheep of My pasture, My people." The commission and the speech formula are cut from the words.
places.words_why: Israel's rulers are pictured as "the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves" while they leave "their flock" unfed, and 34:3 carries the picture on ("eat the fat, wear the wool"). "Woe to" is not part of the picture.

places.why: The living water is carried on to 4:14 ("whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst... a fount of water springing up to eternal life"). The narration and His request for a drink, which was literal, are not part of the picture.
places.words_why: "Living water" is the picture carried through to 4:14 ("a fount of water springing up to eternal life"). The rest of the marked clause ("you would have asked Him") is plain speech.

"the fields, for they are ripe for harvest" starts the harvest picture, and 4:36 carries it on ("gathers a crop for eternal life"). The saying "There are still four months until the harvest" is about the real crop.

places.why: The food that lasts is the start of the bread picture that runs through John 6 ("I am the bread of life"). The closing sentence about the seal is plain speech, so it is cut.
places.words_why: "Food that endures to eternal life" begins the bread picture that runs through John 6. "Food that perishes" is real food, and "which the Son of Man will give you" is plain speech.

places.why: The root and branches go on into the olive tree of 11:17-24 ("some branches have been broken off... grafted in"). The dough is a separate picture that is not carried on, so it is cut.
places.words_why: "the root" and "the branches" begin the olive tree picture, and 11:17 carries it on ("some branches have been broken off ... grafted in"). The "if" and "is holy" are not the picture itself.

places.why: Waking up starts the night and day picture of 13:12-14 ("The night is nearly over... put on the armor of light... clothe yourselves"). The opening and closing clauses are plain statements.
places.words_why: "Wake up from your slumber" begins the night and day picture of 13:12 ("The night is nearly over ... put on the armor of light"). "The hour has come" is plain time language.

places.why: The leaven is carried through 5:7-8 ("Get rid of the old leaven... keep the feast... unleavened bread of sincerity"). "Your boasting is not good" and the frame "Do you not know that" do not carry the picture.
The tent and the dwelling are carried through 5:2-4 ("while we are in this tent, we groan... clothed"). "Now we know that" only leads in, so it is cut.
places.words_why: The tent and house picture is plain ("the earthly tent we live in is dismantled ... an eternal house in heaven") and goes on in 5:2 ("in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed"). The "if" and "we have" do not carry it.

places.why: The warfare is carried through 10:4-5 (weapons, strongholds, taking every thought captive). "though we live in the flesh" is plain speech, so it is cut.
places.words_why: The war picture is plain and carried on in 10:4-5 ("The weapons of our warfare... demolish strongholds", "take captive every thought"), but the words that carry it are "wage war", not "do not" or "according to the flesh".

places.why: The church promised in marriage to Christ is a plain metaphor. It is not carried through a passage, because 11:3 turns to a likeness with Eve, so the form is metaphor, not a picture carried through. "I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy" is plain speech, so it is cut.
Paul names the figure himself in 4:24: "These things serve as illustrations, for the women represent two covenants." "For it is written that" only introduces the quotation, so it is cut.
Sowing and reaping are carried through 6:8-9 ("sows to please his flesh... in due time we will reap a harvest"). "Do not be deceived: God is not to be mocked" is a plain warning, so it is cut.

The building picture starts in 2:20 ("built on the foundation... the cornerstone") and goes on to the temple of 2:21. This verse speaks of citizens and a household, which is not plainly the same picture, and the citizenship is not carried on. When in doubt the place does not go live.
Darkness and day are carried through 5:5-8 ("sons of the light and sons of the day... putting on the breastplate of faith"). The address "But you, brothers," is not part of the picture.
places.words_why: The darkness and day picture is plain and goes on in 5:5 ("sons of the light and sons of the day; we do not belong to the night"), but "are not" and "so that" do not carry it.

Right after those who "have fallen away" (6:6), the "land that drinks in the rain ... receives the blessing of God" is plainly a picture, set against the "land that produces thorns and thistles" in 6:8. The opening "For" does not carry it.

The race picture is plain in "throw off every encumbrance" and "run with endurance the race set out for us". The "Therefore, since we are surrounded" clause does not carry it, and reading the witnesses as onlookers comes from commentaries.
The stone picture is plain and carried into 2:5 ("like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house"), but "As you come to Him" is not part of it.

"If you go to the left, I will go to the right; if you go to the right, I will go to the left" plainly turns left and right around. The marking cuts in after "If you go to the", so the whole saying should be marked.

places.why: The right and left hands only describe two men standing face to face. The reversal comes from where they stand, not from a figure, and the marked span also cuts off the last "hand".
This is a boundary note. Tappuah and Manasseh come in the same order both times, so nothing is turned around, and "belonged... belonged" is an accident of English word order.
"Jacob and Esau. I gave Esau... but Jacob" is ordinary narration that takes up the last name first. A careful reader would not see a figure here.

"Hannah and the other Peninnah. And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none" is plain narration that takes up the last name first, the same as Joshua 24:4 and 1 Samuel 24:22. The order is not plainly a figure of speech, so it does not go live.

places.words_why: "the LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart" plainly turns LORD and man around. The marking starts without "the" and stops before "sees the heart", which completes the contrast.

places.why: "David gave his oath to Saul. Then Saul returned home, but David..." tells of two men parting. The name order is just the order of the story, not a figure.
"I will go to him, but he will not return to me" plainly turns I and him around, setting the living father against the dead child. The questions before it do not carry the figure, so they are cut.

places.words_why: "love those who hate you and hate those who love you" plainly turns love and hate around, but the marking leaves off the last "you".

places.why: The two women's claims plainly turn living and dead, and mine and yours, around against each other. The narration in between and "So they argued before the king" are cut.

The king repeats the two claims in reversed order: mine alive and yours dead, then yours dead and mine alive. The old span left out "My son is", the first word turned around, so the words now start there.

The man, LORD, LORD, man order comes only from the BSB's English. The Hebrew has "a good one obtains favor from Yahweh, and a man of schemes He condemns", with nothing turned around. The verse's real figure, opposite lines, already has its own place (proverbs-12-2-opposite-seen), so this one is dropped and not re-formed.

"Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous" repeats no word in the BSB. The reversal is only in the Hebrew roots, and this place has no Strong's tags on them. The span also takes in "both are detestable to the LORD".
Verse 14 has only "Seek good, not evil". The reversal needs verse 15's "Hate evil and love good", so this verse does not show it, and the mark is the whole verse.
A plain counterchange: save, then lose; lose, then find. The old mark cut out "save" and "find", which carry it.
A question and an answer that repeat "generation" and "sign". Nothing is counterchanged, the reversed order is only English word order, and the mark takes in "Truly I tell you".
A plain save/lose, lose/save turn. The old mark dropped both "save"s, which carry the figure.
A plain counterchange: save, then lose; lose, then preserve. The old mark left out both ends of the turn.
"You ... support the root" is turned around into "the root supports you". Both "you"s are needed to show who supports whom.

places.words_why: "he who was a slave ... is the Lord’s freedman. Conversely, he who was a free man ... is Christ’s slave" plainly turns slave and free around. The marking takes the whole verse, including "For" and "Conversely". It is cut to the two clauses that are set against each other.

places.why: Rich, poor, poverty, rich: a plain counterchange between Him and you. The opening "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that" is not part of the figure.

places.words_why: "judgment without mercy" is turned around in "Mercy triumphs over judgment", which is a plain reversal. The clause "will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful" only sits between the two halves, so it is cut.

places.why: The judge/law order looks reversed only because of English word order. The law is the thing judged both times, and the verse sets doer against judge, so no counterchange is plain.
Loving is set against not loving. "Death" and "love" keep the same roles in both halves, so no words are turned around.
The BSB has the finished question "How long will it be?", so a reader sees no break. The marked words are the BSB's own filling-in, and there are no Strong's tags.
In the BSB "How long will this go on?" is a finished question. The claimed break is only in the Hebrew and has no Strong's tags, and the whole verse is marked.
The BSB's own dots show the speakers stop mid-sentence. The narration after it, about why they were afraid, is not the figure.
In the BSB, "I am unworthy" is Jacob's plain, literal confession. The Hebrew "I am small" is not shown and has no Strong's tags, so no belittling figure is plain.

Moses is not asking who he is. The question says he is not fit to go, so it is plainly a question that is not asking. It magnifies nothing else, so it is not meiosis. The whole question is marked, without the narration.

"the youngest in my father's house" is Gideon stating his place as a fact. It belittles nothing in order to magnify something else, and the mark leaves out the matching "weakest in Manasseh".

"the smallest tribe of Israel" states a plain fact, since Benjamin was the smallest tribe. Saul's humility is in the questions around these words. No word is made smaller than it is, so the figure is not plain.

"Who am I, and what is my family ... that I should become the son-in-law of the king?" is a humble question that does not really ask. It holds no belittling word such as "dog" or "flea", so calling "Who am I" belittling to exalt depends on reading in the implied answer. When in doubt, drop.

"Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?" is a humble question that does not really ask. The marked "Who am I" holds no belittling word, so the label "belittling to exalt" comes from interpretation rather than from the words. When in doubt, drop.

places.words_why: "You have made Your servant king ... But I am only a little child": a king plainly makes himself small beside the great task and the "people too numerous to count". The words that carry it are "only a little child", without the verb "I am".

places.why: "Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?" is the same humble question as 2 Samuel 7:18. "Who am I" carries the question, not a belittling word, so the meiosis label is a reading supplied from outside the words. When in doubt, drop.
"what is man" and "who am I" here are a question, as the sample found of Psalm 8:4, not a belittling word

The words "What is man that You should exalt him" come right after "Leave me alone" and are Job's complaint about God watching him so closely. Belittling one thing to magnify another is not plain in them; most readers would see a question that is not asking. When in doubt, drop.

"what is man that You are mindful of him" is plainly a question that is not asking, which is what the marked words carry. They hold no belittling term such as "dust" or "grasshopper", and v5 goes on to say "You crowned him with glory and honor". Reading it as belittling done to magnify something else is an inference, so in doubt it fails.

"His anger is fleeting, but His favor lasts a lifetime" sets opposites side by side, and the shortness may be meant literally ("Weeping may stay the night"). These lines carry an opposite, not a plain belittling, and "His anger is fleeting" on its own carries neither.

"my lifetime as nothing before You" laments how short life is (39:4, "how fleeting my life is"). It does not plainly make life small in order to exalt something else, and the marked words are not a clean likeness either. In doubt, so it is dropped.

Right after "Trust in Him... God is our refuge" (62:8), men are made into a vapor that rises on the scale, so that God alone is seen as the one to trust. The span had cut "Lowborn" from the subject, so it now covers the whole clause.

"I was a brute beast before You" confesses past folly. It is not plainly a belittling meant to exalt another, but it is plainly a metaphor: the psalmist says he was a beast. The span is now the word used for him, "a brute beast".
"He is mindful that we are dust" gives what man is made of as the reason for God's pity. It is a plain statement, not a lessening made so that something else is seen as greater.
"what is man" and "who am I" here are a question, as the sample found of Psalm 8:4, not a belittling word

places.words_why: "Man is like a breath" is a plain likeness. The words that carry it are the likeness with its "like", so "like a breath" is enough and "Man is" can go.

places.why: The long desolation of 54:1-7 is called "a moment" and set against "everlasting kindness". The hiding is made small so that the compassion is seen as greater. The span broke off at "everlasting", so it is now "for a moment".

"for I am only a child" is an excuse, which the LORD rejects in 1:7, and it may be literally true of a youth. Jeremiah does not make himself small so that another is seen as greater. The span also opened with "for".
"small among the clans of Judah" describes Bethlehem as it was, in the word's ordinary meaning. The contrast with the coming ruler is real, but no word is made smaller than it is.

"even the dogs eat the crumbs" takes up Jesus' implied picture of children and dogs (15:26). Reading it as a belittling meant to exalt another needs a commentary, and "even the dogs eat" is not what carries the figure.
"take the children's bread and toss it to the dogs" is a picture saying in which the peoples are not named. Nothing in it is plainly made small so that something else is seen as greater.
"even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs" carries on the picture saying. Belittling to exalt is not plain, and the span breaks off on "under".

"I am not worthy to have You come under my roof" is the centurion's plain statement of humility. It does not put one thing down by a figure in order to raise another, and a reader would not see meiosis here without being told.

"We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty" can be read literally: servants who only did their duty earned no thanks (17:9). The verse never names what would be exalted, so belittling to exalt is in doubt.

John makes himself small to lift up the One coming after him: "I am not that One. But He is coming after me whose sandals I am not worthy to untie." Untying sandals was a slave's task, so the verse itself plainly shows the belittling and the exalting. The marked words should take in "sandals", which carries the lowering.

"Our present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us" is a plain comparison of worth. No belittling word or image is used for the sufferings, so no figure is plainly seen.

places.words_why: After "compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord", Paul says "I consider them rubbish, that I may gain Christ", plainly making all things small to magnify Christ. The word that does it is "rubbish", not the verb "I consider them" before it.

places.why: Meiosis is not shown: no belittling word is used. The words are plainly a question that is not asking, wonder that God should care for man, and no other place marks it. The marked words should be the whole question, not the fragment "What is man that", and they leave out the narration "But somewhere it is testified in these words".

"Though now for a little while you may have had to suffer grief in various trials" plainly states how long the trials last. No belittling figure is plain in the verse, and the marked words run on into "you may have had to suffer".

"After you have suffered for a little while" set beside "His eternal glory" plainly states a difference in time. Unlike "light and momentary affliction", no belittling word is used, so the figure is not plain enough to go live without a named writer.
